new_statements.quote: In Cree, stress is non-distinctive: i.e., it never keeps two otherwise id[entical] words apart as in the case of English, permit — noun, versus permit — verb. There are, however, clearly marked degrees of stress; and for the first unit in particular, and for longer utterances, these have been marked as an aid to memory: (') is used to show the strongest stress on a word or phrase. (') is used to mark the next to strongest. (Ellis 1983:36) [Cook continues:] From the stress marked by Ellis in the text on page 71, stress is indeed unpredictable, although the strongest stress is quite frequently on the antepenultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Ellis, C. Douglas. 1983. Spoken Cree: West Coast of James Bay. Revised edition. Edmonton: Pica Pica Press, p. 36 -- as quoted verbatim in Cook, Eung-Do. 1991. Lexical derivation and stress in Cree. In William Cowan (ed.), Papers of the Twenty-Second Algonquian Conference, 21-29. Ottawa: Carleton University, p. 22 (Cook's gloss on Ellis's marked text p. 71 follows the quotation)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Acrobat Paper Capture text layer) and rendered PDF page 2 (= printed p. 22) as an image. The block quotation is there exactly as reported, introduced by "Ellis, describing the dialect of Cree spoken on the west coast of James Bay, says:" and closed "(Ellis 1983:36)": "In Cree, stress is non-distinctive: i.e., it never keeps two otherwise identical words apart as in the case of English, pérmit — noun, versus permít — verb. There are, however, clearly marked degrees of stress; and for the first unit in particular, and for longer utterances, these have been marked as an aid to memory: (´) is used to show the strongest stress on a word or phrase. (`) is used to mark the next to strongest." Mino…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ellis states no positional rule: stress is non-distinctive, but audible degrees of stress exist and are marked in the pedagogical text (strongest and next-strongest) as a memory aid, i.e. presented as something to be learned per utterance rather than derived. Cook's reading of Ellis's marked text is that placement is unpredictable, with the strongest stress most often on the antepenultimate syllable. (Cook's own antepenultimate-stress rule, with penult surface cases from i-deletion, is argued on Plains Cree data, not Moose Cree.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Ellis marks a 'next to strongest' degree with a second diacritic in the marked texts; no rule for its placement is stated. Cook marks only the strongest stress and says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated by Ellis; Cook: 'stress is indeed unpredictable, although the strongest stress is quite frequently on the antepenultimate syllable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Ellis's marking is on 'a word or phrase' within units and 'longer utterances' of a spoken-language course, i.e. connected speech, not citation forms; Cook explicitly notes 'what Ellis deals with is textual material, not individual lexical items'. The statement covers the composite west-coast-of-James-Bay variety (Moose Factory l-dialect plus Fort Albany n-dialect), not Moose Cree alone.
new_statements.identity_note: The only located stress statement is Ellis's, for 'the dialect of Cree spoken on the west coast of James Bay'. Ellis's Spoken Cree (1962/1983/2000) is a composite of the l-dialect of Moose Factory (= Moose Cree, moos1236) and the n-dialect of Fort Albany/Kashechewan (= Swampy Cree, swam1239); Wolfart 1973: fn. 10 says 'in Ellis, 1962 the text shows l' (i.e. the printed forms are Moose Cree), and Ellis 1995 (Introduction p. xiii) defines Moose Cree as the l-dialect of Moose Factory, Swampy Cree as the n-dialect north of Moosonee, and 'Kashechewan Cree' as a mixed n-l usage. The same Ellis 1983:36 statement is already the pending wishlist item for swam1239, so the two records would rest on one source. Cook 1991's own data (antepenultimate rule) are Plains Cree from northern Alberta (plai1258), not Moose Cree.

sources.note: Editorial Conventions pp. 371-377 give the Moose Cree phoneme inventory (12 consonants, 4 long + 3 short vowels), contraction, glides, voicing, phonemic and stylistic variation, but state no stress placement rule; stress is mentioned only in passing ('p, c and k... may be voiced... between a long, stressed vowel and a short one', p. 372). Text notes (p. 402, an n-dialect text) remark 'âsiniy: /â/ is long on the recording, with phonetic stress on the penultimate' and give pitch contours of two interjections. Introduction pp. xiii-xiv identifies Part III texts as l-dialect Moose Cree of Moose F…
